chest: Low, steady larynx, like the start of a yawn. Feel the vibration in your chest. Steady air, no pushing.
nasal: Anti-nasal check: halfway through the note, pinch your nose. If the sound changes, air is leaking through the nose — lift the soft palate (think “yawn”).
open: Mouth open vertically (two fingers), tongue relaxed behind the lower teeth. Round, dark sound coming out of the mouth.
steady: Even volume from start to end. Land straight on the note, no scoop from below, no forced vibrato.
messa: Messa di voce: start piano, swell to mezzo-forte in the middle and return to piano. The pitch does not move.
e: Open E (as in “bed”), not a closed “ay”. Keep the mouth corners loose: a forced smile pulls the sound into the nose.
u: Rounded lips and lots of space inside the mouth. U slips into the nose easily — keep it in the mouth.
trans: Change only the mouth shape. Pitch and volume stay the same and the vowels flow into each other without breaks.
glide: A continuous slide like a siren, no steps. Same vowel and same intensity from bottom to top.
octave: On the way up, lighten the weight instead of pushing; the resonance shifts by itself. Avoid breathy falsetto.
scale: Centre each note before moving on. Legato: the notes connect without hiccups.
arp: Clean leaps: hear the target note in your head before you leave. Don’t slide between notes.
phrase: Sing it like a real recording: long vowels, short consonants, clear diction. Only natural vibrato.
speech: Speak 15–20 cm from the microphone in your conversational voice. No announcer voice: real intent, natural pace.
question: The intonation rises at the end of the question. Let the rise be real, not theatrical.
emphasis: Give the underlined words more energy and length, without shouting. The rest of the sentence stays natural.
emotion: Feel the emotion before you start. RVC learns the colour of your voice in each state.
tones: Tone 1 high and level · Tone 2 rises · Tone 3 dips and rises · Tone 4 falls from the top. Listen to the contour in the tone generator.
retro: Retroflexes (zh, ch, sh, r): tongue tip curled back, touching the roof of the mouth behind the ridge.
alveolar: z, c, s: tongue close to the teeth. j, q, x: tongue flat against the palate, lips in a slight smile.
umlaut: ü: say “ee” and round your lips without moving the tongue.
sandhi: Sandhi: two third tones in a row — the first one sounds like tone 2 (nǐ hǎo → ní hǎo). The generator already plays it that way.
phrasezh: Speak slowly with well-marked contours. Clarity beats speed.
plos: Aspirated plosives: an audible puff right after the consonant. Turn the mouth slightly off-axis so it doesn’t overload.
th: TH: tongue tip between the teeth. Voiceless in “think/three”, voiced in “that/those”.
rl: Alternate R and L with a loose tongue. The vowels stay open and oral.
vw: V: upper teeth on the lower lip. W: rounded lips, not touching the teeth.
sib: Short, light sibilants. Avoid the long, harsh “s” — the dataset will thank you.
top: A note near your top. Light, without squeezing the throat. If you have to push, lower the fine adjust: a strained take teaches the model strain.
pass: Passaggio zone: let the voice mix and ease off the volume a little instead of pulling the chest voice up.
soft: Pianissimo: little volume, but the note in tune and sustained. If the level is too low, raise the gain rather than moving closer.
belt: Projection: support from the abdomen, open throat, no tearing. Move a hand’s width back from the microphone or lower the gain so it doesn’t clip.
breathy: Breathy, close and intimate, but still with pitch. RVC handles pure whisper badly; here we want air and pitch together.
whisper: Two or three takes like this are enough. Keep some pitch in the voice: pure whisper has no note and teaches the model little.
fast: Fast but clean: short, firm consonants (t, k, p, ch, s). That is what keeps the voice from sounding “mushy” in fast songs.
lyric: A line from your lyrics. Sing it in your range with the song’s intent; the melody here is only a guide.
lyriczh: A line from your Mandarin lyrics. Mark the tones clearly: this gives the model’s index Mandarin phonemes in your own voice.
ngsiren: Semi-occluded vocal tract (SOVPE): mouth almost closed, sound vibrating in nose and lips like the end of “sing”. Slide continuously without steps — it connects chest, mixed and falsetto without tension.
nay: Bratty “Nay” with forward, brassy placement like teasing someone. Narrows the epilarynx, helping the vocal cords close cleanly without muscle force. Moderate volume, never shout.
gee: Crisp “Gee” (gui). The firm “G” consonant prompts immediate clean cord closure, while the narrow vowel prevents the throat from tightening as pitch rises.
mixsus: Mixed voice: less chest weight, more body than falsetto. Moderate volume; if your larynx wants to rise, back off and lighten the vowel.
vowelmod: Vowel modification: start in “Ah” and let the lips round towards “Oh” as you ascend. A narrower vowel prevents acoustic strain and avoids shouting.
falsetto: Clean, focused falsetto with clear tone. Avoid excessive breathiness or pure whispering: the model needs clear fundamental pitch, not leaking air.
flip: Intentional flip (yodel) between chest and falsetto. The break is welcome: it teaches the pitch extractor the exact acoustic boundary between registers.
falsedesc: Start in falsetto and descend smoothly into mixed voice without changing the vowel shape or dropping volume abruptly.
mixphrase: Short sung phrase in mixed voice: long vowels, short consonants. If the top note pinches or strains, drop the fine transpose.
